headline: 30% Cheaper Groceries Without AI or Subsidies Possible
summary: Deleting middlemen in food delivery can cut costs significantly
details: The food delivery market has a high commission fee of 15-30% per order, which is passed on to consumers. By removing this 'discovery tax', prices can drop without needing AI or subsidies.
A new open-source project, the Food Freedom Map, uses a map and catalog to connect consumers with stores and restaurants directly, allowing them to list themselves and their products for free.
The project claims that with a simple script, a city's worth of stores can be migrated onto the map in a weekend, making their products more accessible and affordable to consumers.
This approach doesn't require complex AI solutions or expensive infrastructure; it relies on existing open data and simple normalization of store information.
The goal is to change the incentive structure of the food delivery market, prioritizing consumers and producers over intermediaries.
caption:
Can groceries be 30% cheaper without AI? A new project says yes.

The food delivery market has a high commission fee of 15-30% per order, which is passed on to consumers. By removing this 'discovery tax', prices can drop without needing AI or subsidies.

A new open-source project, the Food Freedom Map, uses a map and catalog to connect consumers with stores and restaurants directly, allowing them to list themselves and their products for free.

The project claims that with a simple script, a city's worth of stores can be migrated onto the map in a weekend, making their products more accessible and affordable to consumers.

This approach doesn't require complex AI solutions or expensive infrastructure; it relies on existing open data and simple normalization of store information.

The goal is to change the incentive structure of the food delivery market, prioritizing consumers and producers over intermediaries.

headline: Go raises $553M in Japan's biggest IPO of 2026 Go eyes robotaxis and acquisitions
summary: Go, Japan's largest ride-hailing app, raised $553M in its IPO to expand robotaxi business and make acquisitions.
details: Go, Japan's largest ride-hailing app, raised ¥88.6 billion ($553 million) in its IPO, the country's largest so far in 2026. The company plans to use the funds to expand its robotaxi business and make acquisitions.

The IPO came during one of Japan's quietest listing seasons, with the government encouraging startups to sell themselves rather than go public. Go drew investments from BlackRock, Wellington Management, and M&G Investment Management.

Japan's taxi industry faces a driver shortage, with a 20% decline in recent years. Go believes robotaxis will be part of its future and has partnered with Waymo, an autonomous driving subsidiary of Alphabet.

Go has 35 million downloads, 85,000 partner vehicles, and an 80% share of Japan's taxi app market by usage time. The company is also exploring partnerships with Kakao T, Alipay, and WeChat Pay to allow inbound travelers to hail taxis directly from their local apps.
